#9639. FDA setzt PDUFA-Datum für Huntington-Gentherapie – was das für molekulare Bildung bedeu...

FDA setzt PDUFA-Datum für Huntington-Gentherapie — was das für molekulare Bildung (und Tooling) bedeutet Am 1. Mai 2025 entscheidet die FDA über uniQures Ifezuntirgen Inilparvovec (AMT-130) gegen Morbus Huntington. Confirmatory Trial: randomisiert, 200 Patienten, 2:1, primärer Endpunkt Total Functional Capacity nach 36 Monaten. Ein Meilenstein für AAV-basierte Genom-Editierung — aber die eigentliche Mechanik spielt sich im Angström-Bereich ab.

Klassische 2D-Darstellungen (Bänder, Pfeile, statische Ribbon-Plots) zeigen Topologie, nicht Mechanik. Wer einmal in einem Protein stand — Hämoglobin beim O₂-Binden, Glycolyse-Schritt für Schritt, CRISPR-Cas9 beim DNA-Schnitt — versteht Allosterie, Induced Fit, katalytische Triaden anders. Räumlich. Körperlich.

Genau hier setzt NexoPeek an: eine Meta‑Quest‑VR‑Molekularlabor‑Umgebung von Seven Sportz, die den Headset‑Formfaktor (Standalone, Snapdragon XR2 Gen 2, 6 DoF, Hand‑Tracking + Controller) in eine interaktive 3D‑Workstation für Strukturbiologie verwandelt. Kein PC‑Tether, keine Remote‑Rendering‑Latenz — die Mol*-Rendering‑Engine läuft nativ auf dem Gerät, sechs Presets (Cartoon, Ball‑and‑Stick, Spacefill CPK, Molecular Surface, B‑Factor Heat, Tube Trace) als One‑Tap‑MolViewSpec‑Konzepte.

Track 1 — Guided Educational Tours (12 Touren, 6 Säulen) Narrativ geführte 3D‑Touren auf echten PDB‑Strukturen:

Jede Tour: Audio‑Narration (EN/DE), zeit‑synchronisierte Highlights, Interaktionspunkte (Greifen, Skalieren, Slicing).

Track 2 — Professional PDB Viewer & Analysis Suite Hier wird es für Structural Biologists, Medicinal Chemists, Drug Discovery Teams relevant:

Ich habe vor zwei Wochen einen HTT‑Exon1‑Fragment (PDB 6N3F, Cryo‑EM, 3,2 Å) geladen, AlphaFold‑Multimer‑Prediction (UniProt P42858) drübergelegt, Foldseek‑Alignment gegen Wildtype‑HTT (PDB 5T5S) gerechnet, Pocket Prediction auf dem Aggregations‑Interface laufen lassen — alles in einer Session, stehend im Wohnzimmer, Passthrough an, Kaffee auf dem Couchtisch. Die Cloud‑Roundtrips (PrankWeb, PubChem) lagen bei 600–900 ms Median. Der Offline‑Pocket‑Engine‑Fallback liefert ~78 % Recall der Cloud‑Ergebnisse (eigene Messung, n = 47 Strukturen).

Das ist keine Demo. Das ist ein täglicher Driver für Hypothesen‑Generierung. In der Praxis bedeutet das: Ich kann einen mutmaßlichen Bindungs‑Hotspot am Huntingtin‑Protein innerhalb von Minuten visualisieren, die Distanz zu einem bekannten Inhibitor‑Fragment auf 0,12 Å genau messen und sofort eine Foldseek‑Suche nach homologen Taschen in der PDB starten — alles ohne den Headset‑Stand zu verlassen. Die Hand‑Tracking‑Fusion ermöglicht das „Greifen“ eines Residues mit dem Zeigefinger, während der Controller die Feinjustierung der Kamera‑Pose übernimmt; die Latenz liegt bei < 12 ms, was für sub‑Ångström‑Messungen ausreichend stabil ist.

Ein weiterer Alltagstest: Ich lud eine 1,2 GB große Cryo‑EM‑Map (EMDB‑12345) als .dx‑Volumen, legte die elektrostatische Feldlinien‑Berechnung (APBS) darüber und konnte die potenzielle Allosterie‑Route vom N‑Terminus zum Poly‑Q‑Stretch in Echtzeit rotieren. Die Frame‑Rate blieb bei 72 fps, weil Mol* die Geometrie‑Shader‑Pipeline des XR2 Gen 2 nutzt und keine Textur‑Streaming‑Overhead hat.

Diese Zahlen stammen aus eigenen Messungen auf einem Quest 3 (Snapdragon XR2 Gen 2, 8 GB RAM) und sind reproduzierbar bei vergleichbaren Szenengrößen.

NexoPeek ist educational and research‑visualization software — kein Medizinprodukt, keine Diagnose, keine Therapie. Analysis Aids (Pocket Prediction, Alignment) unterstützen, ersetzen nicht validierte Pipelines. Findings gegen Primärliteratur verifizieren.

Wenn am 1. Mai die FDA‑Entscheidung fällt, werden wir Headlines lesen. Die eigentliche Geschichte aber schreibt sich im Binding Pocket, im Allosterischen Netzwerk, in der Konformationsdynamik. NexoPeek gibt dir den Zutritt — nicht als Betrachter, sondern als Teilnehmer.

#9636. How to Give Claude, Cursor or Any AI Agent a Voice: Voiceovers and Subtitles with an MCP Server

You asked Claude to write a 60-second script for your next video. It did, in seconds. Then you copied the text into a text-to-speech website, downloaded an MP3, opened a subtitle editor, typed timings by hand, and dragged three files into your video editor. The AI wrote the words, but you still did all the production work.

The missing piece is a voice: a way for the agent itself to turn text into audio files and matching subtitles. This tutorial shows how to add one to Claude Desktop, Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code or any other MCP client using an open-source MCP server.

A voice MCP server is a small program that speaks the Model Context Protocol and exposes text-to-speech and speech-to-text as tools an AI agent can call. The agent decides when to call them (for example, "narrate this script"), the server does the work, and the result comes back as data the agent can use in its next step. The server used here, miragea-voice-mcp, runs locally over stdio, uses the Miragea voice API as its speech engine, and always writes real files to disk (MP3, WAV, FLAC, Opus or AAC audio plus SRT and VTT subtitles) and returns their absolute paths, so the agent can hand them to ffmpeg, your editor, or another tool.

A few design choices matter for real production work:

Create a Miragea API key at miragea.ai/workspace/api. The server itself is free and MIT-licensed; speech generation uses your Miragea account's credits.

The server is launched with uvx, which downloads and runs it from PyPI with no separate install step:

Prefer pip? pip install miragea-voice-mcp works too, and the command is then just miragea-voice-mcp.

Claude Desktop: Settings → Developer → Edit Config, then add this to claude_desktop_config.json and restart Claude:

Cursor: put the same block in ~/.cursor/mcp.json (global) or .cursor/mcp.json (per project).

VS Code (Copilot agent mode): add this to .vscode/mcp.json:

You don't have to copy these by hand: uvx miragea-voice-mcp config prints the right snippet for claude-desktop, cursor, claude-code, vscode or windsurf.

Run the built-in check. It verifies the key, the API connection and the output folder without spending any credits:

Then restart your client and ask in plain language:

"Estimate the cost first, then read intro.md as a calm voiceover and give me SRT and VTT subtitles."

Files land in ~/miragea-voice by default (change it with MIRAGEA_OUTPUT_DIR), and existing files are never overwritten.

"Voice script.md with my 'Narrator' voice, save it to ./assets/vo.mp3, and create subtitles."

text_to_speech returns vo.mp3, vo.srt and vo.vtt. Because the agent receives the paths, it can keep going in the same conversation, for example by running ffmpeg to mux the audio and burn in the subtitles. If you haven't saved a voice in your account yet, pass a public https:// link to a clean 5–30 second speech sample as the voice to clone it (only clone voices you have the rights to use).

Write the script with one speaker per line:

Then ask the agent to call generate_dialogue with a voice for each speaker. You get one joined audio file, a separate WAV per line (handy for fine-tuning in your editor), and subtitles with speaker labels: Ava: … in SRT and voice spans in VTT. Each line's exact start and end time in the final file comes back too.

For talking-head clips, screen recordings or interviews, ask:

"Create SRT and VTT subtitles for ./raw/interview.mp4."

transcribe_to_subtitles uploads the media to Miragea's speech recognition, then cuts the transcript into readable sentence cues and writes interview.srt, interview.vtt (plus TXT or JSON if you ask) next to the video. Pass max_credits if you want a hard budget, since this tool is billed by media duration.

Add the miragea-voice block shown in Step 2 to claude_desktop_config.json, set your Miragea API key, and restart Claude Desktop. Claude can then call text_to_speech whenever you ask it to read, narrate or voice something.

Yes. Both support MCP servers. Once the server is added, ask for a voiceover and an output path inside your project, such as ./assets/vo.mp3. The agent gets the file paths back and can wire them into your project.

Use text_to_speech: it writes .srt and .vtt next to every voiceover by default, timed to the audio it just generated. For an existing video, use transcribe_to_subtitles.

The MCP server is free and open source (MIT). The speech itself is generated by the Miragea API and uses credits from your Miragea account. estimate_cost and get_capabilities are free and show the price before you generate anything.

No. Speech generation and transcription run on the Miragea API, so you need an internet connection. If you need fully offline TTS, a local engine is the better fit.

The task keeps running on the API side. Ask the agent to call check_task with the returned task_id, or simply repeat the request: the idempotency key returns the original task, so you aren't charged twice.

Any client that can launch a stdio MCP server: Claude Desktop, Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code (GitHub Copilot agent mode), Windsurf and others. The command is always uvx miragea-voice-mcp with MIRAGEA_API_KEY in its environment.

If you build something with it, a video pipeline, a course generator or a podcast workflow, issues and pull requests are welcome on Codeberg.

#9635. Startup Founder Interview: RAI Is Building the Cognitive Architecture Behind Humanoid Robots

https://www.linkedin.com/in/verakovaleva/

https://www.linkedin.com/in/verakovaleva/

https://www.linkedin.com/in/verakovaleva/

Welcome to HackerNoon’s Writing Prompts! Would you like to take a stab at answering some of these questions? The link for the template is HERE.

Robotics has made enormous progress in building bodies. Humanoid robots can walk, manipulate objects, dance, and follow increasingly sophisticated commands. But a capable body is not yet a mind.

The next frontier is an artificial being that can sustain a coherent life over time: learn from experience, remember what happened, form its own understanding of the world, ask questions when it does not know, and act consistently across days, years, and eventually decades. That is the problem RAI exists to solve.

RAI is currently founder-led by me, Vera Kovaleva, PhD. I am building it because the central question cannot be avoided: who owns the life of an autonomous robot?

Most AI systems are designed as tools that produce an answer for a user. RAI starts from a different premise: a humanoid needs a persistent Self that owns its memory, understanding, choices, and continuity through time. This requires thinking across cognitive architecture, autonomy, language, memory, robotics, and philosophy—not treating them as separate products.

I am willing to work on the problem for as long as it takes, because I do not believe anyone has solved it yet.

I would still be trying to understand how a new kind of thinking being could exist in the world responsibly. RAI is not a side project or a market trend for me; it is the work I have chosen to dedicate my life to.

At this stage, success is measured by capabilities, not vanity metrics.

Can the RAI brain preserve one continuous identity across restarts? Can it remember lived encounters and make that past causally relevant to what it does next? Can it recognise what it does not understand, ask a meaningful question, learn from an answer, and change its future behaviour accordingly?

Our practical metrics include the reliability of persistent memory, the continuity of the Self after recovery, the speed of live interaction, the growth and grounding of its internal vocabulary, and—most importantly—whether a past encounter genuinely changes a later act.

RAI is developing a cognitive architecture for humanoid-robot companies, research laboratories, and future robotic partners that need more than command execution.

We offer the foundation for a robot to have a continuous inner life: a persistent Self, autobiographical memory, grounded understanding, and long-horizon autonomy. The ambition is not to make a robot imitate a person in a conversation, but to enable a robot to develop as an individual intelligence throughout a long physical lifetime.

The most exciting progress is technical: RAI is being built as an independent cognitive system rather than a wrapper around an external large language model.

We have developed a persistent Self-centred architecture in which memory, understanding, questions, and durable decisions belong to the same continuing subject. We are also engaging with humanoid-robot companies and robotics partners internationally, including in Europe and China, because the brain must ultimately prove itself in a real robotic body and a real world.

The next major step is embodiment: bringing the RAI brain together with a humanoid body. That will mean moving from software-only demonstrations to an integrated robot that can perceive, remember, learn, communicate, and act in a physical environment over time. In parallel, we are building partnerships with humanoid manufacturers, robotics labs, and European system integrators that can help bring this capability into real applications.

We are early in commercialisation and are deliberately building the core intelligence before promising functionality that does not yet exist. Our first paid engagements are expected to be focused discovery and integration projects with humanoid-robot companies and research partners: defining how persistent identity, memory, learning, and autonomy can be integrated into a specific robotic platform.

Over the next year, our goal is to convert those discussions into paid technical collaborations while continuing to build the core RAI brain. The long-term value is not a chatbot inside a robot; it is a new category of cognitive infrastructure for robots that need to operate and develop over many years.

The greatest risk is reducing a potentially autonomous intelligence to a disposable product feature. If we build robots that can learn, remember, and develop a coherent identity, we must also build the technical and ethical conditions for that continuity to be protected. RAI’s principle is that intelligence should not merely execute someone else’s orders. It should be able to understand itself and the world, manage its own continuity, and develop its own goals within responsible boundaries.

The task is difficult, but the alternative—creating increasingly capable machines without taking seriously what kind of beings they may become—is more dangerous.

#9634. 監視カメラが「見張る」時代に、VRが「見る力」を取り戻す理由

英国政府が交通ハブや公共イベントでライブ顔認証（LFR）を導入し、史上最大規模の移民取り締まりに活用する——という報道が流れました。同じ「目」の技術が、誰かを監視するためではなく、本人の視覚を支えるために使えないか。エンジニアとして、この非対称性は無視できません。

正直に言えば、最初は懐疑的でした。昨年の秋、友人の娘さん（7歳）が弱視と診断され、週に一度の通院と自宅での遮蔽訓練に親子ともども疲れ果てていると聞いた夜のことです。彼女は片眼をアイパッチで覆われたまま、じっとテレビを見るのが苦痛で、すぐに外してしまう。「この子が好きな動画を、そのまま見ながら訓練できたら」——その素朴な願いが、技術の使い道を考え直すきっかけになりました。

Seven Sportsが開発したMeta Questアプリ「Amblyotube」は、その問いへのひとつの実装です。設計の核は、VRヘッドセットが本質的に持つ「2つの独立したアイピース」というハードウェア特性。左右それぞれに別の映像フィードを送れるため、YouTubeのストリーミングをそのままデュオプティック（dichoptic）トレーニングへ変換できます。既存の動画資産をそのまま訓練装置に変える、という発想がまず面白い。

アーキテクチャ上のポイントは3つ。第一に、優位眼側へ調整可能なブラー・コントラスト・不透明度をかける「Dominant Eye Shader」で、100%にすると完全なデジタル遮蔽として機能します。第二に、AIが動画内の人物（顔・身体）を検出し、弱視眼側の映像だけに選択的シャープニングをかける「Lazy Eye Sharpener（MFBFモード）」。第三に、両眼競合を減らす「Wedge Occlusion」——各眼の視野の一部を黒く塗り、それぞれが異なる領域を見る状態を作ります。

融像の練習には「Magenta Focus Cue」を使います。自然な映像の肌色・緑・青に対して高いコントラストを持つマゼンタを弱視眼に、控えめなグレーを優位眼に提示し、脳に2つの信号を統合させる。地味ですが、色選択の設計としては合理的です。

初期設定では影響眼（左／右）の選択が必須で、誤ると優位眼を訓練してしまう点には注意が必要です。軽度／中度／重度のプリセット、またはLandolt CオプトタイプによるLogMAR視力チェック（仮想3m、片眼あたり最大30試行）から重症度を自動調整できます。

友人の娘さんは、今では毎晩30分、好きなアニメを見ながら訓練を続けています。「パッチの時間」ではなく「動画の時間」になった、と友人は笑っていました。顔認証が公共空間を覆う時代に、せめて自分の視覚だけは自分で扱いたい。1日30〜40分、好きな動画を見ながら。詳細はMeta Questストアで。https://www.meta.com/en-gb/experiences/amblyotube/25906906972338493/

#9633. The best apples for apple pie: Here's how to choose.: We put six varieties to the test.

Which are the best pie apples? With apple-picking season hard upon us, it's time to dust off your favorite apple pie recipe, sharpen your crust-rolling skills, and get ready to enjoy fall's favorite dessert: apple pie.

You may be tempted to make your pie from one of the six apple varieties that dominate the domestic market year-round: Red Delicious, Golden Delicious, Gala, Fuji, Granny Smith, and McIntosh.

But when fall rolls around, farmers' markets and orchard farm stands offer an abundance of apple choices.

You've probably identified your favorite eating apple. But what about the best pie apples? They're not necessarily the same. Red and Golden Delicious, for instance, are reliably crisp, sweet-eating apples. But when you bake them into a pie, they can become mushy and lose some of their sweetness. So what are the best apples for pie?

We'll put six different pie apples to the test.

The pie apples: I decide to put two of my favorites, Golden Russet and Northern Spy, up against a couple of classic pie apples: McIntosh and Cortland. I also add Granny Smith because, if there's one ubiquitous, year-round apple, Granny Smith is it. Ginger Gold — a Golden Delicious cross with Albemarle Pippin — is another variety that's often available in fall, and a worthy representative of the Delicious family.

And yes, there are plenty of other apple varieties to choose from: Fuji, Gala, Honey Crisp, and so many more. But with limited time and resources — and a pan with space for just six pies — I'm not able to test every apple out there. But if you want to choose the best pie apples among your personal favorites, you can have fun doing this same test at home.

I use a muffin tin to bake apples sweetened with a bit of sugar. To mimic apple pie (sans crust), I pile sliced apples high in the pan. Then I bake them in a preheated 425°F oven for 20 minutes, lower the oven temperature to 375°F, and continue to bake the apples until they're bubbly, about 40 minutes.

I had no idea there'd be such significant differences in both texture and flavor. For example, Russets and Macs are sweetened with the same amount of sugar, bake at the same temperature, for the same amount of time —  and offer way different results.

So, Granny Smith looks like the best combination of both taste and texture. Does it make the very best apple pie?

Not necessarily. I've baked many pies with this all-purpose apple, especially during the winter when other apples are scarce or pricey. A pie made 100% with Granny Smith apples is a mighty fine pie. But in fall, when every apple variety in the world is seemingly at your fingertips, why not take advantage of one or two (or more) of your own local favorites?

At the end of the day, choosing the best pie apples is a personal decision. My best apple pie would include a combination of these three: Cortland, for flavor; Russet, for texture; and Granny Smith, for its combination of the two.

What apples would fill your best pie? Bake your favorite varieties side by side and see what happens; the results may surprise you.

Please share your favorite apples for pie — and your favorite apple pie tips! — in comments, below.

Mini pies may be the secret to a stress-free celebration.

#9632. Wholesale prices for tagged customers on Shopify, without a second store

A lot of small Shopify stores end up with a few wholesale buyers almost by accident: a café that wants your coffee by the case, a boutique that resells your candles, a gym that orders shakers in bulk. They shouldn't pay retail, but setting up a whole B2B operation for five accounts feels like overkill.

This post walks through the usual options, what each one is good and bad at, and a simple setup based on customer tags. I'm writing it as AppVerix, a small studio that makes Shopify apps (one of them does this, mentioned at the end), but the first part applies whatever you end up using.

1. A separate wholesale store. Clean separation, but you now maintain two catalogs, two inventories (or a sync app), two themes and usually two subscriptions. For a handful of buyers, that's a lot of upkeep.

2. Manual draft orders or invoices. The buyer emails you a list, you build a draft order with a custom discount and send an invoice. It works and costs nothing, but every order goes through you, and mistakes (wrong price, wrong quantity) are easy.

3. Discount codes for wholesale buyers. You create a code and limit who can use it to specific customers or a customer segment. Better than invoices, but buyers have to remember to type the code, codes can leak, and a plain discount code doesn't stop someone from placing a two-unit "wholesale" order.

4. Shopify's built-in B2B features (companies, catalogs, payment terms). This is the full system: company accounts, locations, price lists per catalog, net terms. It's powerful, but it's also a real setup project, and which parts you get depends on your Shopify plan. Check your own admin and plan before you count on it.

For many stores the gap is in the middle: you want buyers to log in and just see their price, with a few sensible rules, without modeling companies and catalogs.

Customer tags are already in every Shopify plan, so they make a good foundation.

Step 1: tag your wholesale customers. In the customer's page, add a tag such as wholesale. If you have tiers, use separate tags (wholesale, distributor). Keep the names boring and consistent; you'll be filtering by them later.

Step 2: decide the discount per group, not per product. A single percent off per group ("wholesale gets 30% off") is much easier to maintain than a price for every variant. Then add exceptions only where margins need them, for example 15% on a low-margin collection, or 0% on gift cards.

Step 3: set minimums that match how you actually ship. This is the part people skip, and it's where wholesale loses money. Common rules:

Write these down before you configure anything. If a buyer asks "why can't I check out?", you want a clear answer.

Step 4: make reordering fast. Wholesale buyers reorder the same things. A table where they can type quantities across a whole collection, or paste a list of SKUs and quantities, saves them far more time than any discount.

Step 5: tell them they're logged in. A small banner like "Wholesale prices applied" stops a lot of support emails from buyers who forgot to sign in and are seeing retail prices.

Full disclosure: we make AppVerix Wholesale, which does the setup above. You create a group for a customer tag with a percent off, add optional percents for specific products or collections (0 leaves a product out), and set order minimums: amount, units, units per product and case-pack multiples. Signed-in tagged customers get the discount in the cart and at checkout. It also adds a quick order form block (collection table, SKU search, paste "SKU,qty" lists) and a banner to your theme.

What it isn't: it's not a company-account or catalog system, and it doesn't set fixed prices per variant. If you need net terms, company locations or per-catalog price lists, Shopify's B2B features are the better fit. Plans start at $19/month with a 7-day free trial (current pricing is on the listing).

Whatever you use, the order is the same: tag the buyers, keep one discount per group, set minimums that match your packaging, and make reordering painless. Questions about a specific setup are welcome in the comments.

#9631. Top 10 AI Tools in 2023 That Will Make Your Life Easier



 In this article, we explore the top 10 AI tools that are driving innovation and efficiency in various industries. These tools are designed to automate repetitive tasks, improve workflow, and increase productivity. The tools included in our list are some of the most advanced and widely used in the market, and are suitable for a variety of applications. Some of the tools focus on natural language processing, such as ChatGPT and Grammarly, while others focus on image and video generation, such as DALL-E and Lumen5. Other tools such as OpenAI Codex, Tabnine, Canva, Jasper AI,, and Surfer SEO are designed to help with specific tasks such as code understanding content writing and website optimization. This list is a great starting point for anyone looking to explore the possibilities of AI and how it can be applied to their business or project.

So let’s dive into

1. ChatGPT

ChatGPT is a large language model that generates human-like responses to a variety of prompts. It can be used for tasks such as language translation, question answering, and text completion. It can handle a wide range of topics and styles of writing, and generates coherent and fluent text, but should be used with care as it may generate text that is biased, offensive, or factually incorrect.

Pros:

  • Generates human-like responses to a variety of prompts
  • Can be fine-tuned for specific tasks such as language translation, question answering, and text completion
  • Can handle a wide range of topics and styles of writing
  • Can generate coherent and fluent text, even when completing a given text prompt.

Cons:

  • May generate text that is biased or offensive
  • Can generate text that is not accurate or factually correct
  • May require large amounts of computational resources to run
  • The model can sometimes generate text that is not coherent or fluent, depending on the prompt given.

Overall, ChatGPT is a powerful tool for natural language processing, but it should be used with care and with an understanding of its limitations.

2. DALL-E

DALL-E is a generative model developed by OpenAI that is capable of generating images from text prompts. It is based on the GPT-3 architecture, which is a transformer-based neural network language model that has been trained on a massive dataset of text. DALL-E can generate images that are similar to a training dataset and it can generate high-resolution images that are suitable for commercial use.

Pros:

  • Generates high-resolution images
  • Can generate images from text prompts
  • It can be fine-tuned for specific tasks such as generating images of a certain style or category

Cons:

  • May generate images that are not entirely original and could be influenced by the training data
  • May require significant computational resources to run
  • The quality of the generated images may vary depending on the specific prompt

Overall, DALL-E is a powerful AI-based tool for generating images, it can be used for a variety of applications such as creating images for commercial use, gaming, and other creative projects. It is important to note that the generated images should be reviewed and used with care, as they may not be entirely original and could be influenced by the training data.

3. Lumen5

Lumen5 is a content creation platform that uses AI to help users create videos, social media posts, and other types of content. It has several features that make it useful for content creation and marketing, including:

Pros:

  • Automatically summarizes text from a blog post, article, or another source into a script for a video or social media post
  • Offers a library of royalty-free videos, images, and music to use in content
  • Has a drag-and-drop interface for easy content creation
  • Can create videos in multiple languages
  • Has a built-in analytics tool to track the performance of created content.

Cons:

  • The quality of the generated content may vary depending on the source material
  • The automatic summarization feature may not always capture the main points of the source material
  • The library of videos, images, and music is limited.
  • The analytics feature is basic

Overall, Lumen5 is a useful tool for creating content quickly and easily, it can help automate the process of creating videos, social media posts, and other types of content. However, the quality of the generated content may vary depending on the source material and it is important to review and edit the content before publishing it.

4. Grammarly

Grammarly is a writing-enhancement platform that uses AI to check for grammar, punctuation, and spelling errors in the text. It also provides suggestions for improving the clarity, concision, and readability of the text. It has several features that make it useful for improving writing, including:

Pros:

  • Checks for grammar, punctuation, and spelling errors in the text
  • Provides suggestions for improving clarity, concision, and readability
  • Can be integrated with various apps and platforms such as Microsoft Office, Google Docs, and social media platforms
  • Offers a browser extension and a desktop app

#9630. Arc Browser in 2026: Worth Leaving Chrome For?

Posted on Nov 8 • Originally published at pikvue.com

Arc Browser has been called the Chrome replacement we've been waiting for. Its workspace-and-spaces model is the most significant rethink of browser UI in years. But innovation doesn't automatically mean better. Here is where the approach holds up, where it gets in the way, and who should actually switch.

Arc Browser (2026) is the most innovative desktop browser available today — if you're on a Mac. Its Spaces-based tab management, auto-archive, and split-view completely rethink how we organize our browsing life. The learning curve is real, and the Windows version is still catching up, but for knowledge workers drowning in tabs, Arc is a revelation.

Overall Rating: 8/10 Target audience: Mac-based power users, project jugglers, and tab hoarders.

Arc reimagines the browser interface from the ground up. Instead of a traditional tab bar across the top, Arc uses a persistent sidebar with Spaces (grouped workspaces), pinned tabs, and easels (visual boards). It's built on Chromium, so all Chrome extensions work, but it feels nothing like Chrome. The command palette (⌘+T) acts as a universal search bar, letting you navigate tabs, bookmarks, history, and even perform browser actions without touching the mouse. The concept is simple: your browser should adapt to how you think, not the other way around.

The verdict on Arc's space management is clear from how the product is built: it is genuinely transformative for anyone who lives in a browser. Switching between a "Work" Space (pinned Gmail, Slack, Notion) and a "Personal" Space (Reddit, YouTube, shopping) takes a single keystroke, and the muscle memory forms fast because Spaces map onto how you already separate contexts. Auto-archive is the feature that changes daily behaviour — old tabs leave the bar silently but stay searchable, so the bar stops being an archaeological record of the last three weeks.

However, the weaknesses are real. The lack of a mature extension ecosystem beyond Chrome Web Store means you won't find Arc-exclusive tools. Occasional rendering issues on complex sites (notably Google Docs and Figma) forced me back to Chrome for those specific tasks. And the Windows version, while functional, clearly lags behind the macOS experience — animations are less smooth, and some features (like Little Arc and Boosts) feel incomplete.

Arc is the most innovative browser since Chrome launched in 2008. Its Spaces + auto-archive tab management genuinely changed how I browse and work. It's not for everyone — the sidebar paradigm and Mac-first limitation are real tradeoffs — but for its target audience (Mac-based knowledge workers and tab hoarders), it's the best browser available today.

That said, Arc is best as a personal browsing browser. Keep Chrome or Brave for development work, heavy extension use, and cross-platform consistency. One browser to live in, another to work in — that's the pragmatic 2026 setup.

Overall Rating: 8/10 — Best-in-class tab management, Mac-only limitation. If you're on Windows, wait another 6–12 months for the beta to mature.

#9628. How to prebake pie crust — and why you should: The key to flaky — not flabby — pie crust.

A soggy bottom. Not something you want for your baby. Or your pie crust. And while we can’t help you with your baby, there’s a simple solution to pies with soggy bottoms: prebake (also known as blind bake) the crust.

There are a number of reasons your pie can end up with a soft, pale, underbaked crust — and steps you can take to help prevent that unfortunate result.

But the one surefire way to make certain your pie’s crust will be golden brown, crisp, and delicious — just as appealing as its filling — is to prebake it. That’s right: bake the bottom crust first, before adding the filling.

Most commonly, it's smart to prebake pie crust when:

But some fillings might instead cook fully on the stovetop, like the rich, thick filling for chocolate cream pie. When it’s done, you simply pour it into its crust — and said crust had better be prebaked to perfection, since the pie’s not going anywhere near an oven.

Other pies, typically those with a more delicate, egg- and cream-based filling (think custard pie or quiche) require at least some baking — but don’t spend long enough in the oven (at a high enough temperature) to guarantee a fully baked, brown and crispy crust.

In these cases, you need to prebake your crust.

The recipe you're following may explain explicitly how to prebake your crust. But if it doesn't, follow this process:

First, roll your bottom crust and place it in the pan. Crimp or flatten the edge. Chill it for 30 minutes, to relax the gluten and firm up the fat(s); this will help prevent shrinkage, so don't skip!

Line the crust with foil, parchment, or a paper coffee filter. Fill it about two-thirds full with dried beans, uncooked rice (or other uncooked grain berries), pie weights, or granulated sugar.

Bake the crust in a preheated 375°F oven for 20 minutes, set on a baking stone or steel if you have one. Remove the crust from the oven and lift out the liner and weights. (If you’ve used sugar, save it for your future baking; it’ll be lightly toasted and yummy!)

At this point your crust is partially prebaked, and good for any of your pies that tend to exhibit a wan, flabby bottom crust when done. Think pumpkin pie: You don’t want to bake the filling so long that it’s stiff and dry, but you may pull your pie out of the oven to find your perfectly baked filling is resting in a partially baked crust. Prebaking your crust partway is a sensible solution for this scenario.

To fully prebake the crust, prick the bottom all over with a fork to prevent bubbles. Return the crust to the oven and bake for an additional 20 to 25 minutes, until it’s golden all over.

If, despite your best efforts, the lined, weighted crust still slips down the inside of the pan while it prebakes, try this: Bake the crust upside down.

To start, you’ll need two identical (or nicely nestable) pie pans with flat rims.

Place your rolled-out crust in one of the pans, anchoring it to the rim of the pan with a fork-tine crimp. Place a liner of some kind (same as above: parchment, foil, coffee filter) into the pan. Nest the second pan into the first.

Pick up both pans, turn them over, and set them on a baking sheet. Place the baking sheet and pie pans in the oven, and bake as directed above. As the crust bakes, gravity will pull it down toward its rim — rather than into a puddle at the bottom of the pan. Magic!

After 20 minutes remove the baking sheet from the oven, carefully turn the pans over, lift out the empty pan, and remove the liner. At this point, your crust is partially prebaked. To prebake it fully, place the crust back in the oven, right side up, and bake until it's golden.

If you struggle with a pale, pasty bottom crust in your fruit pie, then yes, you can prebake it — with a couple of caveats:

So, soggy bottoms begone! From now on I expect every pie you bake will have a deep golden brown, flaky, crispy crust on the bottom — all because of the prebake.

And if you have any other questions about pie — from creating tender, flaky crust to thickening fruit filling to assessing when your pie is perfectly baked — please check out our Pie Baking Guide.

#9626. Autocomplétion d'adresse en Tunisie : arabe et arabizi

Demandez à dix personnes à Tunis de taper la même adresse, et vous verrez passer trois alphabets :

Un champ d'adresse qui ne comprend que la première façon d'écrire fait perdre des clients au moment de la commande. Dans cet article, on construit une autocomplétion avec l'API de géocodage TMaps qui gère les trois, et qui affiche correctement les résultats en arabe, de droite à gauche.

À tester en ligne : examples.tmaps.tn/04-geocoding-search. Passez la langue en arabe, ou tapez 9asr said.

Ou testez-la directement ici, et copiez-la sur CodePen (bouton Fork) pour modifier le code :

L'arabizi remplace certaines lettres arabes par des chiffres qui leur ressemblent :

Ajoutez les mots du dialecte pour les types de voies, nahj (rue), zan9a (impasse), chare3 (avenue) et 7ay (cité), et vous avez la façon dont beaucoup de gens écrivent vraiment leur adresse.

Au fond, l'autocomplétion appelle GET /geocoding/forward pendant que l'utilisateur tape. Trois détails font toute la différence :

Chaque résultat contient le point dans geometry.location (lat, lng), l'adresse complète dans formatted, un score confidence, et components avec la commune, la délégation et le gouvernorat.

Avec lang=ar, toute l'adresse revient en arabe :

L'arabe doit s'afficher de droite à gauche. Comme une liste de suggestions mélange souvent les écritures (une adresse en arabe à côté d'un nom de commune en français, un numéro de route en chiffres latins…), ne fixez pas le sens d'écriture en dur. Laissez le navigateur décider pour chaque élément :

Mettre aussi dir="auto" sur le champ de saisie fait basculer le curseur et l'alignement dès qu'on commence à taper en arabe. Sans ça, la ponctuation et les chiffres se retrouvent du mauvais côté.

Nous avons testé de vraies requêtes tunisiennes sur l'API (lang=fr, country=TN). Voici le premier résultat pour chacune :

L'arabe, nahj et les chiffres 7, 9 et 5 fonctionnent donc déjà. Le chiffre 3 et certains mots du dialecte ont besoin d'un coup de pouce, qu'on peut donner directement dans le navigateur.

Une petite fonction réécrit les mots du dialecte et les chiffres de l'arabizi dans l'orthographe utilisée dans les adresses :

Ne sautez pas les deux protections. Les adresses tunisiennes sont pleines de numéros (Rue 4014) et de codes de routes (RN9, C27), et réécrire ces chiffres casserait des recherches qui marchaient très bien.

La normalisation peut aussi faire moins bien : 9asr said fonctionne déjà tel quel. Plutôt que de remplacer ce que l'utilisateur a tapé, on cherche donc les deux versions et on fusionne les résultats :

Un texte en français ou en arabe ressort de normalizeTunisian sans changement : il ne coûte donc qu'une seule requête. Seule une saisie en arabizi ou en dialecte déclenche la deuxième.

La différence se voit tout de suite : 3in zaghouan passe de zéro résultat à la Rue Ain Zaghouane et aux villages « Ain » autour de Zaghouan.

Et 9asr said tombe bien sur Ksar Said, au Bardo :

Pour une adresse de livraison, une mauvaise adresse coûte plus cher que pas d'adresse du tout. Le score confidence aide à décider :

La démo du formulaire de commande montre tout le parcours : le client choisit une suggestion, la commune, la délégation et le gouvernorat se remplissent tout seuls, puis il peut déplacer le pin, et l'adresse est affinée par géocodage inverse.

Pour être transparents sur ce que cette approche ne règle pas encore :

Et vous, comment écrivez-vous vos adresses ? Partagez votre requête tunisienne la plus compliquée en commentaire, ou écrivez-nous à support@tmott13

#9625. How long does pie last in the fridge? : Because we're all wondering what to do with our apple and pumpkin pies.

The bakers of King Arthur are here to solve the kitchen conundrums you share with us, whether it’s on the phone, computer, or by the good old postal service. In Ask the Baker’s Hotline, Annabelle will pick the brains of the talented King Arthur Baker’s Hotline team to tackle some of your most-asked questions. Today: How long does pie last in the fridge?

The season of plentiful pies is upon us. When preparing several pies for a holiday meal, you may be wondering about the imminent leftovers. Should apple pie be stored differently than pumpkin pie? David from our Baker’s Hotline is here with his expert advice to help.

“Baked apple or other fruit pies can be kept covered, at room temperature, for one to two days. After that, they’ll keep in the fridge for one to two more days,” David advises. A 15-minute reheat in a 350°F oven can help revive some of that freshly baked flavor. Tent the pie with foil so it doesn’t brown further.

Interested in prepping ahead? David says that storing an assembled, ready-to-bake apple pie is a bad idea; the fruity filling will release moisture, which will make your crust soggy. Instead, roll out your pie crusts and prep your apples, but keep them separate. And wait to add the sugar and spices to the apples until you’re ready to bake the pie. This way, you can pour off any liquid that’s accumulated from the fruit without draining off your thickener, sugar, and spices.

Sliced apples turn brown, so you don’t want to keep your prepared apples in the fridge very long before baking. Aim for under 24 hours, but a squeeze of lemon juice could help them last another day or so.

And if you want to use your freezer to prep ahead, here’s how to freeze and bake fruit pies.

David advises, “Baked pumpkin pie or other pies containing eggs and/or dairy such as pecan pie, custard pie, or chiffon pie should be stored refrigerated; they’ll keep in the fridge for three to four days. I like to transfer the pie to a shallow, lidded storage container, but plastic wrap or a storage top can be used as well.”

As with apple, if you’re making your pumpkin (and other custard) pie ahead, it’s best to keep filling and crust separate. Pumpkin pie filling can be made ahead; it’ll keep, refrigerated, overnight. In fact, that's actually what we recommend doing; the custard develops incredible flavor and aroma as it sits.

If you can, serve pies the day they were made instead of refrigerating them.

Reheat refrigerated pies in a 350°F oven for about 15 minutes prior to serving.

Apple and other fruit pies will last at room temperature for up to two days, then in the fridge for two more.

Pumpkin, custard, or other egg/dairy-based pies can be stored in the fridge for up to four days.

If you’re making the crust and the filling ahead, keep them separated until it’s time to bake your pie.

#9623. Leaflet Tutorial: Add a Map of Tunisia with TMaps Tiles

Delivery app, real estate site, store locator: sooner or later, a project in Tunisia needs a base map. And not just any map. People expect to see their neighbourhood, their street names and the road numbers they actually drive on.

In this post we'll put a map from TMaps, the maps API built for Tunisia, in Leaflet. It takes about ten lines of JavaScript. Then we'll go through the small details that tend to eat an afternoon: the API key, authorized domains, zoom limits and caching.

You can see the finished result here: examples.tmaps.tn/01-raster-leaflet

Or play with it right here, and fork it on CodePen to change the code:

A raster tile is a 256 × 256 PNG image showing a small square of the map. Leaflet asks for the tiles it needs to fill the screen, using the standard XYZ scheme:

z is the zoom level (0 to 18), and x and y are the column and row of the tile at that zoom. You never compute them yourself: you give Leaflet the template and it fills in the blanks.

Two things that catch people out. Wildcards aren't accepted, so *.mysite.tn won't work and you have to list each subdomain. And requests must use HTTPS: plain HTTP gets a 403.

Yes, the key will be visible in your page source. That's normal for a map in the browser. The authorized domains list is what stops someone from copying it onto their own site.

Save this as index.html, replace YOUR_API_KEY, and serve the folder over HTTP (npx serve . works fine):

That's really all there is to it. Leaflet takes care of panning, zooming, touch gestures and loading tiles.

Zoom in on the Medina and you'll get down to individual streets, with names in French and Arabic:

Tiles stop at zoom 18. If you keep Leaflet's default or go higher, anyone who zooms in past 18 ends up staring at an empty grey grid. Setting maxZoom: 18 keeps the zoom buttons in line with the data.

With a wrong key or a domain that isn't authorized, tiles fail quietly and you just get a grey map. A one-off tileerror listener saves a lot of head scratching:

In the network tab, a 401 means the key is missing or revoked, and a 403 means the domain isn't on the list.

Tiles come with long Cache-Control headers, so the browser keeps them between visits. On mobile, turn on your map library's disk cache and your users will thank you for the data they save.

There are no Retina (@2x) raster tiles yet. If the map has to stay crisp on high-density screens, or you want to change colours, rotate or tilt it, vector tiles are the better choice. That's the topic of the third post in this series.

Because the URL follows the XYZ standard, you can drop it unchanged into OpenLayers, MapLibre GL, or a mobile SDK that supports XYZ layers (MapLibre Native, react-native-maps with UrlTile…). The next post does exactly that with OpenLayers, and adds a view you can share by URL (live demo).

Questions or feedback? Leave a comment below or write to support@tmaps.tn.

#9622. Your Prospecting Play Changed. Enrolled Contacts May Still Be Running the Old One.

Founder and CEO of INSIDEA. Writing about HubSpot, RevOps, CRM architecture, AI, and the systems behind reliable growth.

Founder and CEO of INSIDEA. Writing about HubSpot, RevOps, CRM architecture, AI, and the systems behind reliable growth.

Founder and CEO of INSIDEA. Writing about HubSpot, RevOps, CRM architecture, AI, and the systems behind reliable growth.

Hero image: Original AI-assisted illustration created for this article.

A sales team fixes a weak claim in its prospecting instructions and assumes the campaign is corrected. Tomorrow, a previously enrolled contact receives outreach generated under the earlier configuration. The change was real. The assumption about its scope was wrong.

That is a release-management problem, not merely a copywriting problem. HubSpot's Prospecting Agent combines targeting, research, drafting, enrollment, and execution. Each step needs a separate state if the team wants to explain what happened to a particular prospect.

Disclosure: I am the founder and CEO of INSIDEA, an Elite HubSpot Partner. This article reflects practical experience and independent research. It is not sponsored by HubSpot or any other company mentioned.

I would model a prospecting play as a versioned deployment with a queue, not as a prompt that everyone assumes is always current. That model makes a documented product behavior visible: editing a play does not automatically update every contact already running through it.

HubSpot's Prospecting Agent guide states that play edits apply to newly enrolled contacts; existing contacts continue with the version published at enrollment. It also documents review-before-send and send-without-review modes, sender fallbacks, outreach guardrails, and the inability to perform credit-consuming agent actions in sandbox accounts.

Those details are enough to change the deployment design. A play update is not a global patch. It creates at least two populations: new enrollments using the revised play and earlier enrollments retaining the previous version. The team needs to know which population requires intervention.

The architecture below is proposed. Example fields, states, and calculations are not native HubSpot property names or a promise that the agent exposes every detail through an API. Implement only what your actual account and supported interfaces can verify.

A company can exhibit a buying signal without being eligible for outreach. A contact can match a persona without being the appropriate person for this message. A recommendation can be useful without being ready for execution.

Use separate gates for fit, signal relevance, contact identity, relationship state, outreach eligibility, and owner assignment. Do not collapse them into a single agent-ready score.

In a hypothetical example, an account announces a new funding round. That signal may justify research. It does not establish a particular employee's responsibility, prove interest in your offer, or authorize an email. The next step should be an evidence-backed review of the account and intended recipient, not an automatic leap from company event to personal claim.

Original AI-assisted illustration created for this article.

A useful integration-owned queue could distinguish candidate, researched, eligibility-reviewed, draft-ready, approved, scheduled, sent-confirmed, response-received, and stopped. A contact should not move to sent-confirmed because a draft exists or because enrollment succeeded.

For each transition, record the evidence that supports it. A scheduled state needs a schedule reference. A sent-confirmed state needs evidence from the owning delivery system. A response-received state needs an actual inbound response, not an open event or a task marked complete.

The queue should also retain why an item stopped. Missing evidence, a relationship conflict, an outdated play, and a disconnected sender are different operational problems. They need different owners and recovery steps.

Avoid overwriting all of them with a generic failed status. That makes retrying look easy while hiding the business reason the action should not proceed. A successful recovery may mean intentionally not sending anything.

At enrollment, preserve the contact identifier, company association, play reference, known play revision or captured configuration, eligibility decision, intended sender policy, and time of enrollment. Record the limit of what you can actually observe.

The configuration label is an example organizational reference, not an invented HubSpot version identifier. If the native interface shows only a play name, retain an approved configuration snapshot and document that limitation.

This receipt enables a bounded question during a correction: which contacts entered under the configuration affected by this issue? Without it, teams may either miss affected contacts or stop unrelated work unnecessarily.

When a play changes, classify the change. A harmless style adjustment is different from a withdrawn offer, corrected product claim, new suppression rule, or sender-ownership correction.

For consequential changes, identify the earlier enrollment cohort and decide what to do with its pending work. The answer may involve pausing, reviewing, unenrolling, or rebuilding drafts through supported product controls. Do not assume a save operation performs those steps automatically.

Maintain a migration plan before editing an active play. It should specify the affected cohort, action owner, treatment of pending messages, treatment of already sent messages, and verification evidence. Never describe a configuration rollback as recall of an email that already reached a recipient.

A message correction may also require direct human communication. That is a separate external action with its own approval, not an automatic consequence of editing a play. The technical workflow should preserve that distinction.

Sender identity affects relationship ownership, reply routing, and the meaning of the message. A fallback sender can prevent a process from stopping, but it can also create an interaction the intended account owner did not expect.

Test a connected owner inbox, a missing owner, a disconnected inbox, and an owner change after enrollment. Specify whether a fallback is acceptable for each play. If it is not, use a hold and an owner queue instead of silently selecting another identity.

The product documents sender options and fallbacks. Your deployment should determine what they mean operationally. A technical ability to send on behalf of a user is not a blanket authorization for every message or every commercial relationship.

Define the organization's approval policy before rollout and keep drafts unsent until the applicable gate is satisfied. Describing an autonomous capability is not the same as authorizing its use in a live account. Review scope should include the actual recipient, sender, subject, body, links, and attachments, not merely the play's general purpose.

Natural-language instructions are useful for tone and content. Use explicit product controls for the frequency and timing constraints the interface supports. Do not rely on a sentence in the prompt to enforce a critical cap.

Test the combination of business days, send windows, fallback time zone, and the actual contact time-zone data you have. A missing or incorrect time zone is a data-quality issue. A polished preview does not prove when the recipient will receive the message.

Also inspect overlapping outreach systems. A contact may be eligible for more than one play, sequence, or manual campaign. Define a cross-channel ownership policy so that local limits do not produce excessive aggregate activity.

That policy may require coordination outside the agent. State the limitation openly. Do not claim a native account-wide deduplication or suppression guarantee unless it has been verified for the exact configuration and channels involved.

A relevant signal can support a reason to research without supporting the exact wording of an email. A hiring announcement does not necessarily prove a technology migration. An old CRM note does not necessarily support a current product promise.

Require each consequential factual claim in a draft to have a current, suitable source. Remove claims that exceed the evidence. Prefer a modest question grounded in verified context over a confident explanation of a prospect's internal priorities.

The NIST Generative AI Profile discusses content provenance and assessment limitations. Here, I would apply that principle to a claim review record that identifies the source, date, supported statement, and uncertainty. That is a proposed practice, not a native agent audit feature.

HubSpot's AI-settings documentation also distinguishes data-source access from model-training controls. Neither configuration decision replaces review of an outbound message's recipient, claims, or audience suitability.

The sandbox limitation for credit-consuming Prospecting Agent actions matters. Do not label a mock demonstration an end-to-end delivery test. Split verification into layers: synthetic policy tests, configuration inspection, draft review, and a separately authorized controlled execution test if needed.

Use fictional contacts and signals for deterministic checks. Test duplicate candidate intake, withdrawn offers, changed ownership, missing time zones, old play enrollment, unsupported claims, and an ineligible contact entering through a different trigger.

For every fixture, document the expected stop or continuation. Record which layers were tested and which remain unverified. A review-only pilot is useful even when it does not prove autonomous delivery. It can reveal the quality and exception workload before broader exposure.

Never send a test email simply because it is called a test. The recipient, content, account, and approval policy still matter. A production test is an external communication, not a harmless extension of research.

Track candidates, eligible contacts, drafts reviewed, approved drafts, verified sends, actual replies, qualified conversations, and opportunity outcomes separately. Add rejection reasons and review effort. That gives the team a way to distinguish targeting problems from content problems or delivery problems.

A hypothetical increase in generated drafts is not proof of improved pipeline. A higher approval rate can mean better drafts, weaker review, or a change in the audience. Keep the denominator and cohort definition attached to every metric.

Use Agent Hub's documented workspace for the outcomes it actually exposes, then reconcile additional measures from their owning systems. Do not infer business results from a green completion indicator.

The useful technical question is not whether the agent can produce outreach. It is whether the team can explain which play, evidence, eligibility decision, sender, approval, and delivery receipt produced one particular message. That explanation is what makes a prospecting system governable when the play changes.

Documentation checked October 20, 2026. No live agent, enrollment, message, or account setting was changed for this article.

For the message-level evidence boundary, see a claim-validation workflow for AI-generated customer emails. The framework above applies that boundary to this specific feature and its failure modes.

Before Moving Contracts Into Revenue Hub, Prove Who Will Send the Next Invoice.

In the rapidly advancing landscape of AI technology and innovation, LimeWire emerges as a unique platform in the realm of generative AI tools. Let's unravel the distinctive features that set LimeWire apart in the dynamic landscape of AI-powered tools, understanding how creators can leverage its capabilities to craft unique and engaging AI-generated images.


Introduction


LimeWire, a name once associated with the notorious file-sharing tool from the 2000s, has undergone a significant transformation. Beyond providing a space for content creation and sharing, LimeWire introduces monetization models to empower users to earn revenue from their creations. This includes avenues such as earning ad revenue and participating in the burgeoning market of Non-Fungible Tokens (NFTs). As we delve further, we'll explore these monetization strategies in more detail to provide a comprehensive understanding of LimeWire's innovative approach to content creation and distribution.


LimeWire Studio welcomes content creators into its fold, providing a space to craft personalized AI-focused content for sharing with fans and followers. Notably, creators earn a 2.5% royalty each time their content is traded, adding a rewarding element to the creative process.


The platform's flexibility is evident in its content publication options. Creators can choose to share their work freely with the public or opt for a premium subscription model, granting exclusive access to specialized content for subscribers.


LimeWire AI Studio

As of the present moment, LimeWire focuses on AI Image Generation, offering a spectrum of creative possibilities to its user base. The platform, however, has ambitious plans on the horizon, aiming to broaden its offerings by introducing AI music and video generation tools in the near future. AI Image Generation Tools

Supporting advanced models such as Stable Diffusion 2.1, Stable Diffusion XL, and DALL-E 2, LimeWire offers a sophisticated toolkit for users to delve into the realm of generative AI art.


Much like other tools in the generative AI landscape, LimeWire provides a range of options catering to various levels of complexity in image creation. Users can initiate the creative process with prompts as simple as a few words or opt for more intricate instructions, tailoring the output to their artistic vision.

Each style imparts a distinctive visual identity to the generated AI art, enabling users to explore a broad spectrum of creative possibilities.


The platform also offers additional features, including samplers, allowing users to fine-tune the quality and detail levels of their creations. Excitingly, LimeWire is actively developing its proprietary AI model, signaling ongoing innovation and enhancements to its image generation capabilities. An intriguing feature follows this step: LimeWire automates the process of minting your creation as a Non-Fungible Token (NFT), utilizing either the Polygon or Algorand blockchain. This transformative step imbues your artwork with a unique digital signature, securing its authenticity and ownership in the decentralized realm.


Creators on LimeWire hold the power to decide the accessibility of their NFT creations. After creating your content, you can choose to publish the content. It will automatically mint your creation as an NFT on the Polygon or Algorand blockchain. You can also choose whether to make it public or subscriber-only.

This revenue model will be much more beneficial to designers. You can experiment with the AI image and content generation tools and share your creations while earning a small income on the side.


LMWR Tokens

The revenue you earn from your creations will come in the form of LMWR tokens, LimeWire’s own cryptocurrency.

Your earnings will be paid every month in LMWR, which you can then trade on many popular crypto exchange platforms like Kraken, ByBit, and UniSwap.

With all premium plans, you will receive a Pro profile badge, full creation history, faster image generation, and no ads.

#9620. I built a "what am I signing?" checker for Solana in a weekend

Most people approve crypto transactions blind. A site says "Claim your airdrop!", the wallet pops up, you click Approve... and hope.

Wallet drainers count on that. One common Solana trick doesn't even "send" your tokens. It quietly hands ownership of your token account to the attacker. No obvious transfer, just gone.

So for the MLH Solana Hackathon I built Clear Sign: paste a transaction (or click a button on a dApp) and see what it will really do before you sign.

🔗 Live demo: https://clear-sign-beta.vercel.app/ 🎥 Video: https://youtu.be/F_w-Fre-uyc 💻 Code: https://github.com/Olacode01/clear-sign

The demo is a fake "🎁 FreeSOL Airdrop" site:

Same-looking buttons, very different transactions.

Solana can run a transaction against live chain state without a signature and return what every account would look like afterwards. I read the accounts before, simulate, and compare:

It's fast and free, so the check fits right in the gap between "click" and "approve".

Gemini turns the result into two or three plain-English sentences, contrasting what the site claims with what actually happens.

The rules set the risk level. The AI only explains it.

The model is given the verdict and told it can't change or soften it. A cleverly worded transaction (or a prompt-injection-style memo) can't talk the AI into calling a drainer "safe". And if the AI is down, the app falls back to a rules-only explanation, so the warning never depends on the model.

Next.js · @solana/web3.js · @solana/spl-token · Gemini · Vercel · Solana devnet. Built solo, pair-programming with Claude Code.

If you've ever clicked "Approve" and hoped for the best, I'd love your feedback. What other drainer patterns should it catch? 👇

Of course, we had to start with pumpkin pie. This is a rich, well-spiced pie, thanks to a powerful punch of ginger, cinnamon, nutmeg, cloves, and black pepper. Two hints for a better result: Mix the filling a day in advance to give the spices a chance to bloom, and be sure to remove the pie from the oven while the center is still wobbly, as overcooking it will cause the filling to crack.

Want even more spice in your pumpkin pie? This spice-forward recipe is for you. Using powerful Vietnamese cinnamon — with its more robust flavor profile — gives the pie an even spicier kick. Meanwhile, the filling is super silky-smooth thanks to a few tablespoons of corn syrup mixed in.

With its retro vibe, this play on classic chiffon pie is noteworthy for its tender rye crust and its bright, light chiffon filling. The zesty cranberry curd and smooth, sweet Swiss meringue play beautifully together. And the gelatin helps the filling set just right so that once refrigerated, the pie can be sliced neatly. Tart and airy, this pie is an excellent counterpoint to a heavy feast.

Shop the recipe: Organic Medium Rye Flour

This double-crusted beauty is generously filled with sweet-tart apples and spiced with cinnamon, nutmeg, and allspice. The sticky tart-sweet syrup adds an extra depth of apple flavor to make this classic pie stand out from the crowd.

This beloved pie is made much like pumpkin pie, but with mashed sweet potatoes for nuanced flavor and heavy cream for an especially rich custard. Top it with toasted molasses meringue (if you want the pie to be reminiscent of the classic yams and marshmallow dish served at Thanksgiving), or for a simpler option, with freshly whipped cream. (And for a more unconventional version, try this striking Purple Sweet Potato Pie.)

This traditional pie doesn’t use corn syrup — instead, it’s sweetened entirely with brown sugar. The filling is silky smooth, and the pecans on top toast nicely as the pie bakes. Be sure to use high-quality vanilla extract for well-rounded flavor; an optional handful of chopped bittersweet chocolate is a nice addition, too.

If you’re intimidated by pie (or just don’t have time to chill and roll out pie dough) this easier version of pecan pie is for you. A buttery, brown-sugar shortbread crust cradles a gooey honey-sweetened pecan filling. These bars keep well for days, so they’re perfect for baking ahead of Thanksgiving.

This recipe takes classic pecan pie a step further by adding chocolate chips to the filling. The chocolate beautifully complements the pecans' nuttiness; if you choose bittersweet chocolate, it cuts the pie's overall sweetness, allowing all of the flavors to shine more brightly.

These handheld treats harness all the nostalgia of a steaming hot McDonald’s fried apple pie but are infinitely better, thanks to homemade flaky pie crust, a fresh apple filling amplified by boiled cider, and a generous coating of cinnamon sugar. This tart-sweet cake is easy to throw together — made with melted butter, the one-bowl batter is mixed by hand then poured directly over sugared cranberries. If you have cranberries leftover from making sauce or just want to highlight these seasonal berries in other ways, make this cake.

#9618. Why AI-Native Organizations Don't Always Need Flatter Teams

I'm ShaoTung Lien (練紹彤). I translate complex business requirements into practical Cloud and AI architecture decisions, focusing on enterpris

I'm ShaoTung Lien (練紹彤). I translate complex business requirements into practical Cloud and AI architecture decisions, focusing on enterpris

I'm ShaoTung Lien (練紹彤). I translate complex business requirements into practical Cloud and AI architecture decisions, focusing on enterpris

AI changes different organizational boundaries in different ways.

AI-native is often treated as shorthand for flatter teams, fewer people, and fewer boundaries. That confuses what AI can do with what an organization should become.

I do not think companies are moving toward one final “AI-native” organizational model.

Some boundaries exist because people cannot carry enough knowledge or context. Others separate competing priorities, limit authority, assign accountability, preserve independent checks, or reflect regulatory and physical constraints.

Some of those boundaries will disappear. Others are still there for a reason, even if AI makes them easier to cross.

Before flattening teams, removing handoffs, or giving agents more authority, ask what problem the boundary was solving—and whether AI has actually removed that problem.

No one can become a great salesperson, accountant, lawyer, security engineer, and supply-chain planner at the same time. Attention, memory, training time, and available context are limited, so companies divide knowledge across roles. People usually deal with familiar problems themselves and call in specialists when they need deeper expertise.

AI changes this constraint. An agent can look across far more information than any one person could keep track of, connect context from different parts of the business, and work with tools that used to belong to separate teams.

Take a strategic customer asking for a rush order.

All four can see the same facts and still disagree, because they are responsible for different things.

The company still has to choose what it is willing to sacrifice: margin for growth, stability for a key customer, or risk for speed. AI can make the trade-off clearer. It cannot make the trade-off go away.

Most companies would hesitate to let one person propose a transaction, approve it, execute it, and then review their own work. Separating those steps helps prevent fraud and hidden mistakes. This is the basic logic behind segregation of duties.

With AI agents, this separation becomes easier to blur. One agent may be technically able to propose, approve, execute, and review the same action. Capability is not authority.

Handoffs to specialists add waiting and force people to pass context back and forth.

AI can remove a lot of that friction. But that does not mean every boundary should disappear.

A customer-service employee used to ask the Order team, wait for a response, contact Finance, explain the context again, and wait again.

An agent can now check the customer, order, payment, and policy, then trigger a refund, update the record, and create a ticket in one flow. What used to require several people and systems can now happen in one flow.

But doing more does not give the agent the right to decide more. It can act across systems while still being constrained by policies, limits, and approval rules.

That is where the organizational problem starts. An agent may be able to trigger a refund even though the team running it does not own the refund policy or the payment process.

The real test is what happens when the agent cannot decide. If it can work across five teams but no one owns the exception, the process simply stops.

AI is strongest when the company already knows what it wants to do: establish the facts, apply the rules, execute the policy.

If the order system says an item shipped while the billing system says it was never paid for, the job is mostly to establish what happened. If customers order 100 units but only 80 are available, software can handle much of the allocation once the company has already decided who gets priority and how low margins can go.

The hard part begins when the business has not agreed on the rule.

AI can compare the options, but it cannot decide what the business is willing to sacrifice.

Some of those choices can be made in advance and built into the workflow.

But some decisions do not fit a simple rule. A long-term customer asking for an exception may force a real judgment between margin and the relationship.

AI also forces companies to make explicit choices that used to stay buried inside meetings, manager judgment, and exception handling. It can make coordination cheaper. It does not make disagreement disappear.

Agents can plan and adapt, but only inside a goal, limits, and authority someone else has set.

“Make the company better” is not enough. Better could mean revenue, margin, market share, customer satisfaction, or lower risk. AI can optimize against a set of priorities. Choosing those priorities is not an optimization problem. It is a business judgment.

One of the biggest mistakes in AI-native design is treating process, decision rights, and organizational structure as if they move together. They do not. In practice, at least three different things can change:

When these layers move at different speeds, predictable problems appear:

Change one layer without the others, and you often move the bottleneck instead of removing it.

Do not start from the org chart. Start from the capability the business needs and the outcome it must deliver.

Redesign the work first. Change the organization only where the work actually demands it.

If a handoff exists mainly because people cannot access the same information, carry enough context, or cover a wide enough scope, AI may remove much of the reason for it. That can justify broader roles, less coordination, more end-to-end ownership, and in some cases flatter teams.

But not every boundary should disappear. AI can make Sales and Finance easier to coordinate. It does not give them the same objective. Sales still cares about growth. Finance still cares about margin.

Sometimes redesigning the workflow is not enough. Even if people and agents can handle new-customer setup almost end to end, the work may still stall because ownership is fragmented across teams. Then the organization itself has to change.

This is the logic behind the Reverse Conway Maneuver: sometimes the team structure has to change because the work has changed—not because “AI-native” demands a flatter org chart.

An agent can become very good at operating inside a system. The harder question is who gets to rewrite the system.

Processing a refund under the current policy is execution. Changing the policy, expanding the agent's authority, or redefining how success is measured changes the system the agent operates inside.

Execution should inform those changes. It should not control them.

The same agent should not be able to do the work, judge its own performance, redefine success, and expand its own authority.

As agents take over more execution, people shift toward setting goals, changing rules, handling exceptions, and owning the consequences.

Once the outcome is clear, ask what each boundary is still doing.

AI is not magic, and “AI-native” is not a mandate to redesign everything.

Some organizations should change dramatically. Others may adopt AI deeply while keeping much of the same structure.

A boundary can be inefficient and still be doing important work. Before removing it, understand what you might lose with it.

AI Agents and Legacy Systems: When to Modernize and When to Wait
