#9508. Warning Letters Sent to Online Pharmacies Illegally Selling Schedule II Stimulants

The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) have issued joint warning letters to 2 websites for illegally selling and distributing or dispensing schedule II stimulants, including amphetamine drug products marketed as Adderall.

The warning letters to kubapharm.com and premiumlightsupplier.com state that the websites are selling amphetamine drug products, including Adderall, that are misbranded and in violation of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act. Additionally, by failing to register the online pharmacies with the DEA, despite knowingly or intentionally advertising the sale of controlled substances, these websites are also in violation of the Ryan Haight Online Pharmacy Act.

“These letters are not only a warning to the companies that illegally sell prescription medications, but they also serve as a warning to consumers who have bought or have considered buying medications online without a legitimate prescription,” said DEA Administrator Anne Milgram. “Consumers cannot trust the safety or legitimacy of pills sold on unaccredited sites.”

In a press release, the Agency reinforced its commitment to stopping online operators illegally selling potentially harmful drug products to consumers. “These particular types of online pharmacies also undermine our efforts to help consumers safely purchase legitimate prescription medicines over the internet,” said FDA Commissioner Robert M. Califf, MD. “FDA will continue partnering with DEA in an effort to safeguard public health and protect consumers who need access to these important medicines.”

#9505. ADHD Lacks a Biomarker Test… But Not Scientific Validity

ADHD’s validity is confirmed not by a blood test but by an overwhelming convergence of scientific evidence, including a reliable behavioral phenotype, genetic heritability, measurable life impairments, and more.

The diagnostic legitimacy of ADHD has been vigorously debated in contemporary psychiatry circles. For parents navigating a child’s diagnosis or adults receiving a later-in-life diagnosis, the central paradox is this: ADHD has profound, life-altering symptoms but no definitive biological test, such as a blood panel or a brain scan, to confirm its presence.

This absence of biomarkers is frequently cited by critics who characterize ADHD as a modern social construct, a byproduct of high-pressure academic environments, or a medicalization of normal childhood energy. However, the scientific consensus, codified in the 2021 World Federation of ADHD International Consensus Statements, asserts that ADHD is a valid, highly heritable, and neurobiologically grounded disorder.1

In modern medicine, the gold standard for disease validation is a typically quantifiable, objective indicator of a biological state. When you are sick or injured, you expect a physician to draw blood, perform a biopsy, or order a scan or some other laboratory test. Because this reliance on objective evidence is so deeply ingrained, skeptics and critics of ADHD point to the absence of a definitive biomarker as evidence of its illegitimacy. However, these critics misunderstand (or intentionally ignore) this well-known fact: Many indisputably valid disorders cannot be affirmed with biomarker tests.

In fact, painful and disabling disorders such as migraine headaches, trigeminal neuralgia, myalgic encephalomyelitis, complex regional pain syndrome, interstitial cystitis, and mild traumatic brain injury are indisputably physical, nonpsychiatric medical diseases without biomarkers. What these critics ignore is that most, if not all, nonpsychiatric medical disorders were viewed as disorders long before a biomarker test was available.

Medical science says that we observe suffering, seek to understand its causes and treatments, and ideally, find a biomarker for diagnosis. But in the absence of a biomarker, we still must help those in need.

[Get This Free Download: Unraveling the Mysteries of Your ADHD Brain]

Critics of ADHD as a diagnosis also ignore the fact that psychiatric science has established criteria for what is, and what is not, a disorder. In a 2005 paper, “The Scientific Foundation for Understanding Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder as a Valid Psychiatric Disorder,” I documented how ADHD meets all these criteria.2 Below is a summary.

Does ADHD have a consistent and recognizable pattern of symptoms and functional impairments? Yes. Inattention, impulsivity, and hyperactivity are well defined, and those with ADHD have clear functional impairments, ranging from severe academic problems and poor peer relations to accidental injuries and occupational failure. A trait becomes a disorder when it is associated with significant distress or disability, and most people with ADHD would agree that their condition brings both.

Does ADHD have objective correlates, such as neuroimaging, psychological testing, or biochemical markers? Indeed, many studies have documented impaired performance on neuropsychological tests, small differences in brain structure and function, and genetic variants that increase risk for ADHD. This criterion does not require the correlates to be useful for diagnosis, only that they are more likely to be observed in those with the condition compared to those without.

Though individuals with ADHD are at higher risk for other disorders, the symptoms used to diagnose ADHD are different from those used to diagnose commonly coexisting disorders such as anxiety and mood disorders.

[Get This Free Download: Fight Misinformation with These 11 Facts About ADHD]

Does ADHD have a trajectory across the lifespan? Yes, the continuation of symptoms from childhood to adulthood and the emergence of other disorders associated with ADHD have been well documented.

Is there evidence of a genetic cause for ADHD? Yes, ADHD has high heritability and DNA studies show that most cases of ADHD are caused by the accumulation of many genetic risk variants.

Does ADHD have a predictable and beneficial response to specific therapeutic interventions? Yes, substantial evidence supports the benefit of stimulant and non-stimulant medications as well as parent behavior therapy for children and cognitive behavioral therapy for adults.

ADHD’s existence is undeniable. The application of these criteria to ADHD provides a rigorous scientific defense against the claim that the disorder is merely a collection of subjective labels. Its validity is established, not by a simple lab or blood test, but by an overwhelming convergence of scientific evidence: a highly reliable behavioral phenotype, strong genetic heritability, distinct population-level neurobiological correlates, severe and measurable life impairments, and a clear response to medical and psychological treatments. Waiting for a perfect biomarker while children and adults suffer preventable harms would abandon medical responsibility.

Stephen V. Faraone, Ph.D., is a distinguished professor of psychiatry at SUNY Upstate Medical University. He is the founder of the ADHDEvidenceProject.org.

#9503. Two Personality Traits Linked To A Sharper Mind

How you respond to beauty may have more in common with your thinking skills than you realise.

How you respond to beauty may have more in common with your thinking skills than you realise.

Intellectual curiosity and an appreciation of beauty are both linked to stronger thinking skills.

People with these qualities tend to perform better on tests of literacy, numeracy and problem-solving.

The findings suggest that a person’s interest in ideas and aesthetic experiences may offer clues to their cognitive abilities.

Curiosity could encourage people to seek out opportunities to learn, while stronger thinking skills could make exploring complex ideas more rewarding, with both processes reinforcing one another.

Intellectual curiosity involves enjoying ideas, wanting to understand things and being drawn to questions that require thought.

Aesthetic sensitivity describes an appreciation of art and beauty.

Both qualities belong to the broader personality trait of openness to experience, which captures how receptive people are to unfamiliar ideas and experiences.

However, openness also includes creative imagination, and this aspect showed no significant independent association with cognitive performance.

Imagination, curiosity and an appreciation of beauty may overlap in everyday life, but their relationships with thinking skills differ.

The conclusions come from an analysis of almost 68,000 people across 12 countries, including Canada, Germany, Italy and New Zealand.

They completed personality questionnaires alongside assessments of literacy, numeracy and the ability to solve problems as circumstances change.

Intellectual curiosity and aesthetic sensitivity were linked to better performance across all three assessments, even after accounting for other personality traits.

The connections between personality and cognitive skills also varied between countries.

Educational systems and cultural practices could help explain such differences, although the reasons remain uncertain.

Overall, the findings link both a desire to understand the world and an appreciation of its beauty with stronger thinking skills.

The study was published in the journal Large-scale Assessments in Education (Rammstedt et al., 2026).

#9501. ADHD and the Social Processing Gap

“There’s a difference between having social skills and being able to use them consistently in the moment. This is the fundamental challenge for people living with ADHD.”

“Knowing social expectations versus implementing them in real time is a very big challenge for people with ADHD.” — Sharon Saline, Psy.D.

This tension is at the heart of many slip-ups — from oversharing and interrupting to difficulties reading the room — that stump adults with ADHD across various scenarios. Dr. Saline, a clinical psychologist who specializes in ADHD, described this as the “social processing gap” during her October ADDitude webinar, “Reading Body Language & Social Cues: A Primer for People with ADHD.”

Here, learn more about the gap and how to fill it, along with quick tips for navigating sticky social situations with ease and confidence.

ADHD symptoms and traits — like working memory challenges, distractibility, impulsivity, hyperfocus and more — directly impact communication and social skills. But there’s another factor that tends to influence social interactions: shame.

We asked: Which of the following social challenges prompted you to be here today — for yourself or someone important to you? (Select all that apply.)

A history of negative and uncomfortable social interactions means that many adults with ADHD approach social situations assuming they’ll misread a facial expression, take up too much of the conversation, or commit a faux pas. As a result, many are unable to fully participate in conversations without extreme vigilance and/or becoming overwhelmed, anxious, self-conscious, or exhausted.

“ADHD affects our ability to interpret social information when it’s occurring in real time, because of anxiety and rejection sensitivity that complicate those interpretations and how people respond,” Saline said.

Navigating misunderstandings in relationships, friendships, family, and work comes down to three words: Notice. Check. Clarify.

Noticing, or building social awareness, doesn’t mean scanning for signs of disapproval. It is being attuned to other people and adapting to connection, without taking things too personally or making assumptions. “The challenge is to notice these cues without automatically assuming that they’re bored, annoyed, or rejecting us,” Saline said.

That’s where clarification comes in. Uncertainty is a potent trigger for rejection sensitivity, so Saline encourages respectful questioning to address assumptions. For example, if your partner says they’re not upset but their tone sounds irritated, ask, “I’m hearing something different in your tone. Is there something you’d like to talk about?”

#9495. New Research Strengthens the Case for Emotional Dysregulation in ADHD Criteria

The new “severe-combined” ADHD subtype identified in a landmark study is marked by emotional dysregulation, a symptom the DSM-5 doesn’t include in its diagnostic criteria.

When the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM-5) was updated in 2022, officials believed that research was lacking to expand ADHD’s definition to include the common and extremely impairing symptom of emotional dysregulation. Consequently, the overwhelming and uncontrollable emotions reported by many patients remain largely unrecognized as ADHD manifestations.

Now research appears to be catching up to patient reports.

A new landmark study has revealed three ADHD subtypes that reflect neurobiological differences: predominantly inattentive; predominantly hyperactive/impulsive; and the new severe-combined, which is marked by emotional dysregulation.1

Using neuroimaging and computational modeling to map the pathways of ADHD, researchers found that the severe-combined type had 45 areas of brain abnormality tied to emotion and control compared with 26 each for the two other types. The study, which analyzed 1,154 brain scans of children and adolescents with ADHD, was published recently in JAMA Psychiatry.

The findings are “an example of recent insights emerging from neuroimaging that may impact clinical care, which has been an elusive goal,” says F. Xavier Castellanos, M.D., professor emeritus of child and adolescent psychiatry at New York University’s Grossman School of Medicine. He was part of the working group that contributed to the DSM-5.

[Get This Free Download: Emotional Regulation & Anger Management Scripts]

“Still, it’s too early to assume that their intriguing results are real in the sense of replicating repeatedly in independent datasets, particularly by investigators who are not allied or collaborating with the original research team,” says Castellanos. He, like the study authors, calls for prospective studies to validate their biotypes and determine whether they may influence treatment.

Findings that reveal a new severe-combined subtype may come as no surprise to the thousands of parents of children with ADHD, and adults with the condition, who have named emotional dysregulation as the most impairing feature of ADHD in ADDitude surveys.

But, as David Anderson, Ph.D., senior psychologist at the ADHD and Behavior Disorders Center at the Child Mind Institute, points out, parents’ anecdotal feedback precedes scientific validation.

“Finding evidence of a subtype in the brain leaves open questions about the balance of nature versus nurture. Is there a biological basis for subtypes and is it reliable across the span of development?” Anderson asks. “Emotion dysregulation can be biological for kids who are more prone to emotional behavior from an early age, while some are frustrated with the world due to negative feedback they’ve gotten since kindergarten, so it’s environmental. There are multiple pathways to come to this.”

[Read: The Key to ADHD Emotional Regulation? Cultivating Gratitude, Pride & Compassion]

If the study’s findings are replicated, Castellanos says, it would become a new presentation in a future version of the DSM. “I served on the DSM-5 committee, and we were explicitly reminded that the DSM follows the field; it does not lead it. It’s only when the scientific evidence is strongly supportive that DSM changes are allowed. Otherwise, it’s too disruptive.”

Stephen V. Faraone, Ph.D., distinguished professor at SUNY Upstate Medical University, said he believes that emotional dysregulation was not included in the DSM-5 because it might have made differential diagnosis with anxiety and mood disorders more difficult, especially in primary care. He also said he was skeptical that ADHD can be divided into biological subtypes, adding that underlying ADHD brain mechanisms exist along a spectrum and do not fall neatly into separate categories.

The study’s researchers said the findings may eventually create a path toward developing personalized therapeutic strategies.

Carole Fleck is Editor-in-Chief at ADDitude magazine.

#9491. Rising Fentanyl Use Challenges Current Methadone Induction Protocols

An increasing number of PAs and nurse practitioners (NPs) are working in addiction medicine including opioid treatment programs (OTPs) where they are increasingly able to practice autonomously. A recently released commentary in the Journal of Substance Abuse Treatment highlights the challenges that practitioners at OTPs face in reaching therapeutic doses of methadone for patients who are using fentanyl instead of heroin.1 The commentary authors noted that with “fentanyl’s increased potency when compared to other opioids, many papers have described the need for higher doses of methadone to achieve the therapeutic goal of reducing and suppressing opioid withdrawal and subsequent illicit ongoing fentanyl use.”

The commentary authors make several key observations and related recommendations. One key finding is that patients using fentanyl who enter OTPs may view the increased time needed to achieve an effective dose of methadone as evidence that methadone treatment will not work for them, and that this may serve as yet another barrier to treatment.

Current guidelines for methadone treatment by the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA) recommend a maximum initial dose of 30 mg per federal OTP regulations, which were established before synthetic opioids became the leading cause of opioid-involved deaths in the United States. Guidelines state that the dose may be increased by 5 mg to 10 mg every 3 to 5 days. This dosing schedule may be ineffective for patients using fentanyl given their higher tolerance; it may take up to a month or more to reach an effective methadone dose in these patients.

The commentary authors offer several points to consider when adapting induction protocols to meet the therapeutic needs of patients using fentanyl and noted that change can be achieved without lengthy regulatory reform. The authors offer evidence from several US studies in which a more rapid methadone induction schedule allowed achievement of therapeutic doses more quickly without an increase in the risk for overdose, which is highest risk during the first few weeks of methadone induction in OTP settings.

This evidence indicates that OTP providers are attempting to address these concerns with a variety of induction variations, suggesting that more research focused on patients using fentanyl is needed.

This commentary is valuable in attempting to spur further innovative efforts to adapt the methadone OTP model to meet the challenges presented by the greater potency of fentanyl. Engagement early in induction can be challenging for any patient with opioid use disorder seeking treatment. Even before the rise in fentanyl use, many patients with opioid use disorder struggled with the induction period when they were initiated on doses that do little early on to suppress withdrawal symptoms, which are common. This problem is even greater now with the rise in fentanyl use, and this commentary demonstrates the need for OTPs to offer a model for how OTPs and OTP regulators can design more effective induction protocols that are both safe and effective.

This article originally appeared on Clinical Advisor

Buresh M, Nahvi S, Steiger S, Weinstein ZM. Adapting methadone inductions to the fentanyl era. J Subst Abuse Treat. 2022;141:108832. doi:10.1016/j.jsat.2022.108832

#9486. When Your Loved Ones Are Your Child’s Biggest Critic

ADDitude readers share the hurtful ways family and friends treat their neurodivergent children, from spewing ignorant comments to purposefully excluding them, and how they combat them.

ADHD understanding has improved in recent decades, but many people still just don’t get it – and sometimes those people are the ones closest to us.

Hearing your child criticized or misjudged hurts. Hearing criticisms and barbs from family members and friends who don’t understand ADHD ushers in a complicated whirlwind of emotions. You may feel like an inadequate parent. You may worry whether your child will be accepted at family get-togethers. You may grow weary of explaining your child’s condition.

If this is you, you’re not alone. More than 73% of ADDitude readers say they have relatives or friends who criticize or dislike their neurodivergent child. Read about their experiences and how they navigate them below.

“The older generations are close-minded or under-educated about ADHD and make it seem like it’s made up or an excuse. They say, ‘Everyone says they have ADHD’ or ‘You need to be a better parent.’ I am mostly there to protect my children and correct the person who says it, so my kids don’t feel they are less than.” – Gina, California

“I had a friend who would sugar up my kids intentionally to ‘prove’ that I was over-reacting about the negative side effects of sugar. When the kids misbehaved, she blamed it on my ‘inconsistent parenting’ and not the ADHD brain on sugar and food-coloring!” – An ADDitude Reader

[Get This Free Download: 13 Parenting Strategies for Kids with ADHD]

“We’ve had to deal with side remarks at times from relatives and friends. One example would be someone making retorts to their child like ‘Hey, what are you doing? Even John Doe (my son) would behave better than you right now.’ It’s using my son’s negative behaviors as a frame of reference that my wife and I don’t find helpful at all.” – Jono, Canada

“When my daughter was younger, I was still learning how to handle her behavior, but having family and others say that she was out of control, and that I let her get away with behaviors, really hurt. It made me feel like a bad parent. It took years of working with therapists for me to understand that her behavior and diagnosis were not my fault.” – Deneise, West Virginia

“They just don’t seem to understand that ADHD behaviors aren’t always choices. The only solution seems to be limiting time with the people who don’t understand. Plus, now that the kids are older. I explain to them that some people don’t understand.” – Jenny, Virginia

“My sister-in-law criticizes the amount of ‘stuff’ my children have and their ongoing projects. She doesn’t understand that ADHD brains organize differently and create on a whim, or that having the freedom to be creative is where they excel. I usually head off these comments by talking up their creativity and explaining that they are just brilliantly wired differently.” – An ADDitude Reader, Kansas

“My grandparents and siblings definitely thought we were failing at parenting for a while, and a few friends thought I was a bad mom. Most comments centered on not having strict enough rules/seeing my children’s behavior as bad or rude choices vs. dysregulated behaviors. My village now is almost entirely made up of parents of neurodivergent kids, and we’re all so supportive and understanding of how hard everyone works to provide support and education for our children.” – Acadia, Virginia

“My parents say my child is just lazy in school, and he needs to put more effort into everything. So sometimes I just stop telling them the details. For example, in addition to ADHD, my son recently got diagnosed with dyslexia. I won’t tell them. It’s unfortunate, because he is their grandson and they should know, but I just don’t want to discuss it anymore.” – An ADDitude Reader

“I remind them that they have never parented a child with ADHD, so they do not know what it is like to walk in my shoes. I have also sent them articles about ADHD.” – Sarah, Indiana

“Our dearest friends of 20+ years stopped inviting us to their home for Thanksgiving after a particularly difficult time in their home with our children… The best I have been able to engage with them about this is to ask how their nephew who lives in a different city and is also neurodivergent is doing. When they share difficult times in his regard, I focus the discussion on the antecedents to the disruptive behaviors and try to engage them in problem-solving sleuthing. I connect the conversation with my own experience and invite them to do the same. I have had some deep and meaningful conversations with them over the years, but we still are no longer invited to their home.” – Robyn, North Carolina

“I eventually just cut my family off from contact. The pain they caused my kids was not worth maintaining those relationships.” – Christina, Arizona

#9485. Speaking Faster Can Make You More Persuasive — Until This Happens

Your best argument may lose its edge if listeners struggle to keep up with how quickly you deliver it.

Your best argument may lose its edge if listeners struggle to keep up with how quickly you deliver it.

Speaking at a lively pace can make a strong argument more convincing, but rushing can weaken its impact.

Very fast speech makes it harder for listeners to weigh up what they hear, reducing the advantage that good reasons have over weak ones.

The findings suggest that persuading someone depends partly on giving them enough opportunity to think.

The conclusions come from six experiments involving almost 4,000 people who listened to persuasive messages delivered at different speeds.

Across the experiments, increasing the pace from very slow speech initially improved impressions of the speaker’s confidence and encouraged closer consideration of the message.

However, these benefits eventually weakened or reversed as the delivery became faster.

This helps explain why simply telling someone to speak more quickly is incomplete advice.

A faster delivery can make an argument easier to engage with until the listener begins struggling to keep up.

Crucially, the consequences depend on whether the reasons being offered stand up to scrutiny.

In the two main experiments, listeners heard a proposal that would allow university students to pay lower tuition fees in exchange for working part-time.

Some heard strong arguments emphasising benefits such as smaller classes and better services.

Others heard weak arguments that included reduced leisure time and superficial improvements to the campus.

The recordings were digitally altered to change speaking speed while keeping other vocal features, such as pitch and intonation, unchanged.

Participants then rated their support for the proposal, with some also recording the thoughts that had occurred to them while listening.

The combined results showed that strong arguments gained an increasing advantage over weak ones as speech became faster, but lost some of that advantage at higher speeds.

In other words, delivery affected how effectively listeners distinguished a convincing case from an unconvincing one.

A central part of persuasion is how carefully people consider the reasons they are given.

When listeners examine a message closely, they have more opportunity to recognise its strengths, spot its weaknesses and form their own reactions.

This benefits a strong argument, while exposing the shortcomings of a weak one.

Very fast delivery can interfere with that process, making the merits of the message less influential.

The analyses suggested that changes in how easily listeners felt they could follow the reasoning helped explain this pattern.

Although speaking speed also affected how confident the speaker sounded, confidence alone did not adequately explain the overall pattern.

One possible reason very slow speech is less effective is that it makes sustaining attention more demanding, while excessively fast speech leaves too little time to absorb the content.

The experiments tested seven speaking speeds, ranging from 113 to 218 words per minute, but did not establish one ideal pace.

The most effective delivery is likely to depend on factors including the complexity of the message, the audience and the presence of distractions.

The findings also concern recorded persuasive messages, so they do not establish a universal rule for every conversation or public speech.

For someone presenting a strong case, the findings suggest keeping the delivery lively while giving listeners time to follow the reasoning.

Rushing may reduce the very scrutiny that would otherwise make a good argument convincing.

The study was published in the Journal of Nonverbal Behavior (Guyer et al., 2025).

#9484. Early Puberty More Common in Girls with ADHD

Neurodivergent girls are more likely to experience early puberty and may be especially vulnerable to its effects. Here, understand why.

Puberty is not a single event, but a years-long process that is both universal and highly individual. It shapes brain and emotional development, identity, and lifelong physical and mental health. If it begins before a child is developmentally ready, it can increase the risk for physical and mental health problems.

Research suggests that girls with ADHD are more likely to enter puberty early and to experience the transition more intensely, placing them at heightened risk for anxiety, depression, eating disorders, and other challenges. Parental guidance, emotional regulation skills, and professional support can buffer these risks by bolstering self-confidence in girls as they navigate the pubertal transition.

Researchers are examining why girls with ADHD have about twice the risk for early puberty, and why autistic girls are up to four times more likely to experience early puberty compared to other children.1 In addition to higher rates of obesity and social stress, which could accelerate the onset of puberty, neurodivergent girls may experience differences in dopamine activity, stress response, and immune and neuroendocrine systems — all of which may affect sexual development.

Early relative puberty — development that begins earlier than average but remains within the typical age range — is different from precocious puberty. In girls, precocious puberty refers to physical and hormonal changes before age 8, including breast and pubic hair development, rapid growth, and menstruation. It requires medical evaluation and treatment. Left unmanaged, it can contribute to shorter adult height, psychosocial distress, and other complications. Two forms exist:

[Get This Free Download: Learn How Hormones Impact ADHD Symptoms]

When estrogen and progesterone rise in girls, ADHD symptoms fluctuate. Here’s how:

Rising hormone levels affect the physiological and neural systems involved in emotional processing and regulation.

Girls who menstruate may also experience pronounced changes in ADHD symptoms across the menstrual cycle.

Girls who mature early may feel distressed when their physical development outpaces their cognitive, emotional, and social development.

[Read: The Menstrual Cycle Impacts ADHD Symptoms in Disparate Ways]

“I can’t control the wind, but I can adjust my sails.”

“I can notice this moment without judging it.”

What activity could give my mind a break?

“I can choose where to place my attention.”

Molly Nikolas, Ph.D., is an associate professor in the Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences at the University of Iowa.
